newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Ssangyong Motor gets help from affiliate.
newsitem.headline: Ssangyong Motor gets help from affiliate.

text.p: A key affiliate of South Korea's Ssangyong Group raised payment guarantees to its struggling auto unit, which planned to convert bonds to stocks to improve its cash flow, a group spokesman said on Friday.
Analysts said Ssangyong's moves plus a possible capital increase by its German partner Daimler-Benz AG would temporarily resolve the crisis.
The spokesman said Ssangyong Oil Refining Co had decided to raise payment guarantees to its affiliate Ssangyong Motor to 180 billion won ($202 million) from 100 billion.

Ssangyong Oil, the major shareholder of the automobile affiliate, announced the decision after the refiner's major shareholder, Saudi Arabia's state-oil company Saudi Aramco, agreed to the guarantee hike, he said.
Ssangyong Oil has a 33.3 percent stake in Ssangyong Motor, while Saudi Aramco owns 35 percent of the refiner.

He said Ssangyong Motor planned to convert 100 billion won worth of Ssangyong Motor convertible bonds to stocks next month and issue an additional 100 billion won worth of convertible bonds in the second half of this year, he said.
"This will improve Ssangyong Motor's financial status and solve the current fund shortage," he said.
Analysts said the conversion of convertible bonds would increase Ssangyong Motor's shareholders' equity and improve its debt-to-equity ratio.
The Ssangyong spokesman said it hoped to reduce Ssangyong Motor's debt-to-equity ratio to 1,400 percent by the end of 1997, from the current 2,400 percent.
The automaker's debt-to-equity ratio stood at 10,496 percent at the end of last year, according to Korea Investor's Service.
"The 1,400-percent ratio would still be very high compared with the nation's average corporate ratio of 300-400 percent," said Lee Sang-hoon, an auto analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Securities.
"But the conversion would mean no more interest payments on the bonds, which is good for the company," he said.

Kim Byong-seok, a banking analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities agreed: "The conversion of convertible bonds could help the company look better for financial institutions when they go through the credit-screening process."
However, analysts said the relief appeared temporary given Ssangyong Motor's poor business performance.
Ssangyong Motor has suffered huge losses from massive investments in new models.
Ssangyong's debts are currently estimated at 3.2 trillion won. The nation's four-wheel-drive utility vehicle maker incurred losses of 228.5 billion won in 1996 on sales of 1.37 trillion won.
Analysts said a possible capital expansion by Daimler-Benz AG could also provide a cure for the cash-starved Ssangyong Motor.
Ssangyong Group said on Thursday the two sides were in talks on increasing the German firm's stake in the auto company.
A senior Ssangyong Motor financial manager has said the two companies had tentatively agreed that Daimler-Benz would raise its stake in Ssangyong to 45 percent or more from the current 2.55 percent.
Spokesmen of the two companies denied any agreements had been reached so far.
Analysts doubted Ssangyong Group would ever give the German firm managerial control of the South Korean automaker.

"The group leaked the talk of capital increase in order to stabilise its stock prices, which had fallen sharply on rumours of cash flow troubles," said Huh Ghang, an auto analyst at Hyundai Securities.
"Ssangyong Group has no intention of giving up management rights to the automaker. It has so far only shown strong attachment towards the firm."
